title: Carrying a hazard-ratio bias into net benefit: the extrapolation family moved the decision more than the bias did
question: Does propagating a bias-corrected hazard ratio and its interval into an economic model reproduce the decision uncertainty, or does the bias need to share a parameter space with the extrapolation model?
design: Decision model with Weibull or cure control survival, a log hazard ratio bias elicited on [-0.15, 0.15], three treatment-effect extrapolation families; point propagation, scenario analysis and a joint probabilistic reference.
answer: No. The probability of negative net benefit was 0.38 under point propagation of the reported hazard ratio and 0.67 when the bias (log hazard ratio within 0.15) and the treatment-effect extrapolation family were varied jointly. Almost all of the difference came from the extrapolation: a symmetric bias region alone moved the probability to 0.42, while a waning or cure extrapolation reversed the decision at the reported estimate. The worst joint combination (net benefit -9,618) was worse than any one-at-a-time scenario (-6,657).
findings: Reversal probability by family, joint over the bias: persisting 0.42, waning 0.82, cure 0.75.
Net benefit moved roughly linearly and symmetrically in the bias within each family, so a symmetric bias region barely changes the reversal probability.
Scenario analysis as currently recommended missed the joint worst case.
not_answered: Deterministic survival curves instead of fitted extrapolations; three families, no splines; one symmetric bias parameter; costs and utilities fixed; one price. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Probability of negative incremental net benefit (decision reversal)
methods_compared: joint probabilistic analysis over bias and extrapolation family
